Whether he actually did that or if it's just a thought experiment is still debated by historians, but the principle holds. Acceleration due to gravity is independent of mass in a vacuum. Of course, if you go to the moon, it's only about one-sixth of that. The Apollo astronauts had to learn how to walk all over again in that low-gravity environment. Energy is a fascinating concept, though, when you move away from the biological and look at the physical. In mechanics, energy is simply defined as the capacity to do work. You have potential energy—like a boulder sitting at the top of a hill—and kinetic energy, when that boulder is actually rolling down. The formula for kinetic energy is one-half mass times velocity squared. It’s very elegant in its simplicity. But then you get into electrical energy, which is what really runs our modern infrastructure. The whole War of the Currents in the late 1880s between Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla is a perfect example of... of commercial interests clashing with scientific optimization. Edison was pushing for direct current, DC, which is fine for short distances, but it suffers from severe voltage drop over long transmission lines. Tesla, who was backed by George Westinghouse, championed alternating current. With AC, you can use transformers to step up the voltage for long-distance transmission, which minimizes power loss, and then step it back down for safe residential use. The Chicago World's Fair in 1893 was completely illuminated by Westinghouse using Tesla's AC system, which pretty much proved its superiority once and for all. It completely changed the trajectory of human civilization... 

But, um... as for me, personally? No, no unusual energy. I just keep a steady pace.
